1.f3 e5 2.e4.strategy: Puts a pawn in the centre and frees the queen and the king's bishop, as 1.e4 would have done without the weakening move. The pawn on f3 still takes the knight's natural square and leaves the e1–h4 diagonal open, so Black has the more pleasant game.

1.f3 e5 2.Kf2.strategy: A provocation rather than a plan: the king gives up castling and steps onto the open diagonal, where ...Qh4+ and ...Bc5+ are both check at once. Black only has to develop sensibly and make use of the exposed king.
1.f3 e5 2.Kf2.name: Barnes Opening: Hammerschlag
1.f3 e5 2.Kf2.background: In 2020 Magnus Carlsen played 2.Kf2 against Wesley So in a blitz game. So said it was humiliating when someone plays f3 and Kf2 and just crushes you.

1.f3 e5 2.g4.strategy: Walks into the fastest possible mate: 2...Qh4# ends the game on the spot, because the pawns on f3 and g4 have opened the diagonal to the king and nothing can block it or give the king a square.

1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#.strategy: Checkmate on the second move. The queen reaches h4 along the diagonal that f3 and g4 have opened, the king has no flight square, and no White piece can interpose or capture the queen.
1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#.name: Barnes Opening: Fool's Mate
1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#.background: The fool's mate was named and described in The Royal Game of Chess-Play, a 1656 text by Francis Beale that adapted the work of Gioachino Greco. It is the fastest checkmate in chess, and it can occur only if White commits an extraordinary blunder.
